content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/smaschek/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/7.0.2/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.

dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.

superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|

| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |

| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |

# SMA-831: upgrade jiff to 1 as a breaking change of core and the facade

Linear: [SMA-831](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-831/upgrade-jiff-to-10-as-a-breaking-change-of-paigasus-helikon-core).
Size: a small change. This is the short design.

## Intent

jiff 1.0.0 was released on 2026-11-15. Dependabot PR #363 bumped the
requirement as a `chore(deps)` change, which release-plz releases as a patch.
That is wrong: `jiff::Timestamp` is public API of `paigasus-helikon-core`
(the `ts` fields of the `SessionEvent` variants). A user who builds a
`SessionEvent` with a jiff 0.2 `Timestamp` breaks after the upgrade. The
upgrade must be released as a minor bump.

## Goals

- The workspace requires jiff `1`. `Cargo.lock` has jiff 1.x only.
- release-plz makes a **minor** bump of `paigasus-helikon-core` (0.6.0 → 0.7.0).
- release-plz makes a **minor** bump of the facade `paigasus-helikon`
  (0.6.x → 0.7.0). The facade re-exports core, so the facade break is the same
  break. (Sven's decision, 2026-11-20. It differs from the 0.5 → 0.6 precedent,
  where the facade got a patch.)
- The CHANGELOGs of core and the facade tell users to upgrade to jiff 1.
- All required CI gates pass.

## Non-goals

- No minor bump for the other crates that use jiff (evals, runtime-agentcore,
  sessions-sqlite, sessions-testkit). They use jiff only internally and get the
  normal patch "update Cargo.toml dependencies".
- No change to the general cascade policy (dependents of a core minor get a
  patch). That is a separate question.
- No move of jiff from `[dependencies]` to `[dev-dependencies]` in
  sessions-sqlite, although its `src/` does not use jiff. Separate cleanup.
- No fix for the five `trybuild_ui` mismatches in core. They fail the same way
  on clean `main` with local rustc 1.99.0, and they are not from this change.

## Anti-goals

- The release PR shows a patch bump of core or the facade.
- The JSON format of a stored `SessionEvent` changes, so old session rows
  cannot be read.

## Constraints and facts found

- A probe compiled the whole workspace (`--all-features --all-targets`) with
  jiff 1.0.1 and no source change. The lockfile moved jiff, jiff-core,
  jiff-static to 1.0.1 and jiff-tzdb, jiff-tzdb-platform to 1.0.0.
- The `serde_roundtrip` snapshot tests of core pass, so the stored format does
  not change.
- jiff-static 1.0 pulls `syn` 3.x next to `syn` 2.x. `deny.toml` has
  `[bans] multiple-versions = "warn"`, so `deny` does not fail on it.
- jiff 1.0 needs Rust 1.85. The workspace MSRV is 1.94.
- release-plz gives a commit to a crate only when the commit changes files in
  that crate's directory. A change to the root `Cargo.toml` alone gives no
  commit to core.
- On a 0.x crate, release-plz turns a breaking commit (`!` after the type, or a
  `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer) into a minor bump, and a `feat` into a patch.
- release-plz keeps hand-written text under `## [Unreleased]` and moves it into
  the release section (precedent: PR #351, the `### Security` notes).

## Approaches

- **A. Breaking marker on the squash commit (picked).** The PR title is
  `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1`. The upgrade notes in the core and
  facade CHANGELOGs make the commit touch both crate directories, so release-plz
  gives the breaking commit to exactly these two crates. Risk: if the `!` is
  removed from the title before the merge, the bump falls back to a patch.
- **B. Hand-bump core and the facade to 0.7.0 in the PR.** Rejected: the
  release-plz cascade does not run for a hand bump, the `[workspace.dependencies]`
  pins need hand edits, and the PR publishes on its own merge.
- **C. Rely on cargo-semver-checks.** Rejected: it is not certain that it
  detects a major-version change of a type from a dependency.

## Design

1. Root `Cargo.toml`: `jiff = { version = "1", features = ["serde"] }`. Replace
   the comment above it. Keep the SMA-818 reason (a caret requirement, not an
   exact pin). Drop the 0.2.29 / RUSTSEC-2026-0173 history, because it applies
   only to 0.2. Keep the statement that `jiff::Timestamp` is public API of core,
   so the next jiff major is a breaking change of core and the facade.
2. `cargo update -p jiff` so the lockfile has jiff 1.x only.
3. `crates/paigasus-helikon-core/CHANGELOG.md` and
   `crates/paigasus-helikon/CHANGELOG.md`: add an `### Upgrade notes` section
   under `## [Unreleased]`. The note says: the `ts` fields of `SessionEvent` now
   have the type `jiff::Timestamp` from jiff 1; code that builds a
   `SessionEvent` with its own `Timestamp` must change its `jiff` requirement
   to `1`; code that uses the constructors that set `ts` to now (for example
   `SessionEvent::user_message`) needs no change; the stored JSON format does
   not change, so old rows stay readable. Link the jiff 1.0 changelog for the
   APIs that jiff itself renamed.
4. mdBook and READMEs: the only jiff reference is
   `docs/book/src/concepts/sessions.md` (`ts: jiff::Timestamp`), with no
   version. It stays correct. No README mentions jiff. No edit.
5. Verify the bump before the PR: in a scratch clone at the branch head, with
   the commit message rewritten to the planned squash title, run
   `release-plz update` and check that core and the facade go to 0.7.0 and the
   other changed crates get patches.
6. The PR title is `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1`. The PR body says
   that the `!` drives the minor bump and must stay in the title.

## Left to the builder

- The exact wording of the comment and the CHANGELOG notes (ASD-STE100 style).
- How to set up the scratch clone for step 5.
- Dependabot can open a new jiff PR on Monday 06:00 UTC. If this PR is not
  merged by then, close the Dependabot PR. After the merge, the requirement is
  `1`, so Dependabot does not propose jiff 1.0 again.

  that crate's directory. A change to the root `Cargo.toml` alone gives no
  commit to core.
- On a 0.x crate, release-plz turns a breaking commit (`!` after the type, or a
  `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer) into a minor bump, and a `feat` into a patch.
- release-plz keeps hand-written text under `## [Unreleased]` and moves it into
  the release section (precedent: PR #351, the `### Security` notes).

## Approaches

- **A. Breaking marker on the squash commit (picked).** The PR title is
  `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1`. The upgrade notes in the core and
  facade CHANGELOGs make the commit touch both crate directories, so release-plz
  gives the breaking commit to exactly these two crates. Risk: if the `!` is
  removed from the title before the merge, the bump falls back to a patch.
- **B. Hand-bump core and the facade to 0.7.0 in the PR.** Rejected: the
  release-plz cascade does not run for a hand bump, the `[workspace.dependencies]`
  pins need hand edits, and the PR publishes on its own merge.
- **C. Rely on cargo-semver-checks.** Rejected: it is not certain that it
  detects a major-version change of a type from a dependency.

## Design

1. Root `Cargo.toml`: `jiff = { version = "1", features = ["serde"] }`. Replace
   the comment above it. Keep the SMA-818 reason (a caret requirement, not an
   exact pin). Drop the 0.2.29 / RUSTSEC-2026-0173 history, because it applies
   only to 0.2. Keep the statement that `jiff::Timestamp` is public API of core,
   so the next jiff major is a breaking change of core and the facade.
2. `cargo update -p jiff` so the lockfile has jiff 1.x only.
3. `crates/paigasus-helikon-core/CHANGELOG.md` and
   `crates/paigasus-helikon/CHANGELOG.md`: add an `### Upgrade notes` section
   under `## [Unreleased]`. The note says: the `ts` fields of `SessionEvent` now
   have the type `jiff::Timestamp` from jiff 1; code that builds a
   `SessionEvent` with its own `Timestamp` must change its `jiff` requirement
   to `1`; code that uses the constructors that set `ts` to now (for example
   `SessionEvent::user_message`) needs no change; the stored JSON format does
   not change, so old rows stay readable. Link the jiff 1.0 changelog for the
   APIs that jiff itself renamed.
4. mdBook and READMEs: the only jiff reference is
   `docs/book/src/concepts/sessions.md` (`ts: jiff::Timestamp`), with no
   version. It stays correct. No README mentions jiff. No edit.
5. Verify the bump before the PR: in a scratch clone at the branch head, with
   the commit message rewritten to the planned squash title, run
   `release-plz update` and check that core and the facade go to 0.7.0 and the
   other changed crates get patches.
6. The PR title is `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1`. The PR body says
   that the `!` drives the minor bump and must stay in the title.

## Left to the builder

- The exact wording of the comment and the CHANGELOG notes (ASD-STE100 style).
- How to set up the scratch clone for step 5.
- Dependabot can open a new jiff PR on Monday 06:00 UTC. If this PR is not
  merged by then, close the Dependabot PR. After the merge, the requirement is
  `1`, so Dependabot does not propose jiff 1.0 again.

# SMA-831: upgrade jiff to 1 as a breaking change of core and the facade

Linear: [SMA-831](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-831/upgrade-jiff-to-10-as-a-breaking-change-of-paigasus-helikon-core).
Size: a small change. This is the short design.

## Intent

jiff 1.0.0 was released on 2026-11-15. Dependabot PR #363 bumped the
requirement as a `chore(deps)` change, which release-plz releases as a patch.
That is wrong: `jiff::Timestamp` is public API of `paigasus-helikon-core`
(the `ts` fields of the `SessionEvent` variants). A user who builds a
`SessionEvent` with a jiff 0.2 `Timestamp` breaks after the upgrade. The
upgrade must be released as a minor bump.

## Goals

- The workspace requires jiff `1`. `Cargo.lock` has jiff 1.x only.
- release-plz makes a **minor** bump of `paigasus-helikon-core` (0.6.0 → 0.7.0).
- release-plz makes a **minor** bump of the facade `paigasus-helikon`
  (0.6.x → 0.7.0). The facade re-exports core, so the facade break is the same
  break. (Sven's decision, 2026-11-20. It differs from the 0.5 → 0.6 precedent,
  where the facade got a patch.)
- The CHANGELOGs of core and the facade tell users to upgrade to jiff 1.
- All required CI gates pass.

## Non-goals

- No minor bump for the other crates that use jiff (evals, runtime-agentcore,
  sessions-sqlite, sessions-testkit). They use jiff only internally and get the
  normal patch "update Cargo.toml dependencies".
- No change to the general cascade policy (dependents of a core minor get a
  patch). That is a separate question.
- No move of jiff from `[dependencies]` to `[dev-dependencies]` in
  sessions-sqlite, although its `src/` does not use jiff. Separate cleanup.
- No fix for the five `trybuild_ui` mismatches in core. They fail the same way
  on clean `main` with local rustc 1.99.0, and they are not from this change.

## Anti-goals

- The release PR shows a patch bump of core or the facade.
- The JSON format of a stored `SessionEvent` changes, so old session rows
  cannot be read.

## Constraints and facts found

- A probe compiled the whole workspace (`--all-features --all-targets`) with
  jiff 1.0.1 and no source change. The lockfile moved jiff, jiff-core,
  jiff-static to 1.0.1 and jiff-tzdb, jiff-tzdb-platform to 1.0.0.
- The `serde_roundtrip` snapshot tests of core pass, so the stored format does
  not change.
- jiff-static 1.0 pulls `syn` 3.x next to `syn` 2.x. `deny.toml` has
  `[bans] multiple-versions = "warn"`, so `deny` does not fail on it.
- jiff 1.0 needs Rust 1.85. The workspace MSRV is 1.94.
- release-plz gives a commit to a crate only when the commit changes files in
  that crate's directory. A change to the root `Cargo.toml` alone gives no
  commit to core.

  release-plz cascade does not run for a hand bump, the `[workspace.dependencies]`
  pins need hand edits, and the PR publishes on its own merge.

  detects a major-version change of a type from a dependency.

   not change, so old rows stay readable. Link the jiff 1.0 changelog for the
   APIs that jiff itself renamed.

   `docs/book/src/concepts/sessions.md` (`ts: jiff::Timestamp`), with no
   version. It stays correct. No README mentions jiff. No edit.

   the commit message rewritten to the planned squash title, run
   `release-plz update` and check that core and the facade go to 0.7.0 and the
   other changed crates get patches.

# SMA-831: upgrade jiff to 1 as a breaking change of core and the facade

Linear: [SMA-831](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-831/upgrade-jiff-to-10-as-a-breaking-change-of-paigasus-helikon-core).
Size: a small change. This is the short design.

## Intent

minor bump.

- release-plz makes a **minor** bump of `paigasus-helikon-core` (0.6.0 → 0.7.0).
- release-plz makes a **minor** bump of the facade `paigasus-helikon`
  (0.6.14 → 0.7.0). The facade re-exports core, so the facade break is the same
  break. (Sven's decision, 2026-11-20. It differs from the 0.5 → 0.6 precedent,
  where the facade got a patch.)
- The CHANGELOGs of core and the facade tell users to upgrade to jiff 1.
- A test proves that a sub-second timestamp string that jiff 0.2 wrote still
  reads and writes back to the same bytes with jiff 1.

- No minor bump for the other crates that use jiff (evals, runtime-agentcore,
  sessions-sqlite, sessions-testkit). They use jiff only internally
  (evals `src/run.rs:210`, agentcore `src/a2a/types.rs:51`, testkit
  `src/lib.rs:66,217` are all private). They get the normal patch
  "update Cargo.toml dependencies".
- No change to the general cascade policy (dependents of a core minor get a
  patch). That is a separate question.
- No move of jiff from `[dependencies]` to `[dev-dependencies]` in
  sessions-sqlite, although its `src/` does not use jiff. Separate cleanup.
- No fix for the five `trybuild_ui` mismatches in core. They fail the same way
  on clean `main` with local rustc 1.99.0, and they are not from this change.
- No fix of the `dependencies_update` comment in `release-plz.toml`.

## Anti-goals

- The release PR shows a patch bump of core or the facade.
- Any crate other than core and the facade gets a minor bump.
- The JSON format of a stored `SessionEvent` changes, so old session rows
  cannot be read.

## Constraints and facts found

- A probe compiled the whole workspace (`--all-features --all-targets`) with
  jiff 1.0.1 and no source change. The lockfile moved jiff, jiff-core,
  jiff-static to 1.0.1 and jiff-tzdb, jiff-tzdb-platform to 1.0.0.
- The core `serde_roundtrip` snapshot tests pass with jiff 1. But they use only
  `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`, so they do not prove the sub-second case. Real rows
  hold `Timestamp::now()` values with nanoseconds.

  `[bans] multiple-versions = "warn"`, so `deny` does not fail on it.
- jiff 1.0 needs Rust 1.85. The workspace MSRV is 1.94.
- release-plz gives a commit to a crate only when the commit changes files in
  that crate's directory. A change to the root `Cargo.toml` alone gives no
  commit to core.
- On a 0.x crate, release-plz turns a breaking commit (`!` after the type, or a
  `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer) into a minor bump, and a `feat` into a patch.
  Precedent: `feat(runtime)!: SMA-482 …` (#177) gave runtime-actix,
  runtime-axum and runtime-agentcore 0.1.x → 0.2.0, and the facade
  0.4.26 → 0.5.0. No precedent has `chore!`, so step 6 must prove it.
- The repo sets `squash_merge_commit_title = PR_TITLE` and
  `squash_merge_commit_message = BLANK`. The squash commit on `main` is thus
  exactly the PR title plus ` (#N)`, with no body. Only the `!` in the title can
  carry the breaking marker; a footer cannot.
- `convco check` accepts `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1`. The
  `pr-title` regex (`pr-title.yml:85`) accepts the subject, and earlier `!`
  titles passed the gate.
- CI installs the release-plz CLI **v0.4.3** (release-plz run 44807764156).
  The local copy is 0.3.158, so it is not a valid stand-in.
- release-plz keeps hand-written text under `## [Unreleased]` and moves it into
  the release section (precedent: PR #351, the `### Security` notes).
- SMA-810 and SMA-826 are on `main` and not yet released for core. They join
  core 0.7.0.
- Nothing publishes until the release PR merges (`release-plz.yml:51-62`).

- **A. Breaking marker on the squash commit (picked).** The PR title is
  `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1`. The upgrade notes in the core and
  facade CHANGELOGs make the commit touch both crate directories, so release-plz
  gives the breaking commit to exactly these two crates. Risk: if the `!` is
  removed from the title before the merge, the bump falls back to a patch.
  Step 8 catches that before anything publishes.

  not run for a hand bump, so each dependent's pin and version need hand edits,

   again after it.

   exact pin). Drop the 0.2.29 / RUSTSEC-2026-0173 history, because it applies
   only to 0.2. Keep the statement that `jiff::Timestamp` is public API of core,
   so the next jiff major is a breaking change of core and the facade.

     `jiff::Timestamp` from jiff 1;

   - upgrade core and the facade together, and upgrade them to 0.7. If the
     lockfile still holds facade 0.6 after a `cargo update`, it can hold two
     copies of core. Check with `cargo tree -d -i paigasus-helikon-core`;
   - the stored JSON format does not change, so old rows stay readable;
   - link the jiff 1.0 changelog for the APIs that jiff itself renamed.
5. mdBook and READMEs: the only jiff reference is
   `docs/book/src/concepts/sessions.md` (`ts: jiff::Timestamp`), with no
   version. It stays correct. No README mentions jiff. No edit.

   the branch onto current `origin/main` as one commit with the message
   `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1 (#999)` and no body. Install
   release-plz v0.4.3 and cargo-semver-checks into a scratch root. Run
   `release-plz update` and check the full version table: core and the facade
   go to 0.7.0, every other changed crate gets a patch, no other crate gets a
   minor, and the `[Unreleased]` notes move into the 0.7.0 sections.

   `Cargo.lock`, the two CHANGELOGs, the new core test file (inside

   PR body says that the `!` drives the minor bump and must stay in the title.

   it. Recover with a follow-up `chore(deps)!:` PR that touches both
   CHANGELOGs.

# SMA-831: upgrade jiff to 1 as a breaking change of core and the facade

Linear: [SMA-831](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-831/upgrade-jiff-to-10-as-a-breaking-change-of-paigasus-helikon-core).
Size: a small change. This is the short design.

## Intent

jiff 1.0.0 was released on 2026-11-15. Dependabot PR #363 bumped the
requirement as a `chore(deps)` change, which release-plz releases as a patch.
That is wrong: `jiff::Timestamp` is public API of `paigasus-helikon-core`
(the `ts` fields of the `SessionEvent` variants). A user who builds a
`SessionEvent` with a jiff 0.2 `Timestamp` breaks after the upgrade. The
upgrade must be released as a minor bump.

## Goals

- The workspace requires jiff `1`. `Cargo.lock` has jiff 1.x only.
- release-plz makes a **minor** bump of `paigasus-helikon-core` (0.6.0 → 0.7.0).
- release-plz makes a **minor** bump of the facade `paigasus-helikon`
  (0.6.x → 0.7.0). The facade re-exports core, so the facade break is the same
  break. (Sven's decision, 2026-11-20. It differs from the 0.5 → 0.6 precedent,
  where the facade got a patch.)
- The CHANGELOGs of core and the facade tell users to upgrade to jiff 1.
- All required CI gates pass.

## Non-goals

- No minor bump for the other crates that use jiff (evals, runtime-agentcore,
  sessions-sqlite, sessions-testkit). They use jiff only internally and get the
  normal patch "update Cargo.toml dependencies".
- No change to the general cascade policy (dependents of a core minor get a
  patch). That is a separate question.
- No move of jiff from `[dependencies]` to `[dev-dependencies]` in
  sessions-sqlite, although its `src/` does not use jiff. Separate cleanup.
- No fix for the five `trybuild_ui` mismatches in core. They fail the same way
  on clean `main` with local rustc 1.99.0, and they are not from this change.

## Anti-goals

- The release PR shows a patch bump of core or the facade.
- The JSON format of a stored `SessionEvent` changes, so old session rows
  cannot be read.

## Constraints and facts found

- A probe compiled the whole workspace (`--all-features --all-targets`) with
  jiff 1.0.1 and no source change. The lockfile moved jiff, jiff-core,
  jiff-static to 1.0.1 and jiff-tzdb, jiff-tzdb-platform to 1.0.0.
- The `serde_roundtrip` snapshot tests of core pass, so the stored format does
  not change.
- jiff-static 1.0 pulls `syn` 3.x next to `syn` 2.x. `deny.toml` has
  `[bans] multiple-versions = "warn"`, so `deny` does not fail on it.
- jiff 1.0 needs Rust 1.85. The workspace MSRV is 1.94.
- release-plz gives a commit to a crate only when the commit changes files in
  that crate's directory. A change to the root `Cargo.toml` alone gives no
  commit to core.
- On a 0.x crate, release-plz turns a breaking commit (`!` after the type, or a
  `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer) into a minor bump, and a `feat` into a patch.
  Precedent in this repo: `feat(runtime)!: SMA-482 …` (#177) gave runtime-actix,
  runtime-axum and runtime-agentcore 0.1.x → 0.2.0, and the facade
  0.4.26 → 0.5.0. The `!` title passed `pr-title` and `commits` then, and
  `convco check` accepts `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1` today.
- release-plz keeps hand-written text under `## [Unreleased]` and moves it into
  the release section (precedent: PR #351, the `### Security` notes).

## Approaches

- **A. Breaking marker on the squash commit (picked).** The PR title is
  `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1`. The upgrade notes in the core and
  facade CHANGELOGs make the commit touch both crate directories, so release-plz

- **C. Rely on cargo-semver-checks.** Rejected: it is not certain that it

The spec is at `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-20-jiff-1-upgrade-design.md` in the worktree.

**The design (approach A):**
- The workspace requirement changes to jiff `1`.
- Upgrade notes go under `## [Unreleased]` in the core and facade CHANGELOGs.

**Challenger verdict:** APPROVE WITH CHANGES. It found no blocker.

**What I added to the spec:**
- **A post-merge check (MAJOR).** Before anyone merges the release PR, confirm that it shows core 0.7.0 and facade 0.7.0. If it shows patches, recover with a follow-up `chore(deps)!:` PR.
- **A stronger pre-PR proof (MAJOR).** I squash the branch onto `main` with the exact final title and run `release-plz update` with the CLI version that CI uses. CI uses v0.4.3, and the local copy is 0.3.158, so I install 0.4.3. I then check the full version table. No precedent uses `chore!`, so this step must prove it.

- **An allowed-diff rule (MINOR).** The branch changes no other `crates/*` path, so no other crate gets a minor bump.
- **The SMA-622 contrast (MINOR).** That hand bump was for a crate whose only dependent is the facade. Core has about 17 dependents, so a hand bump does not fit here.

**What I rejected:**
- **The risk that the squash drops the `!` (MAJOR).** The repo sets `squash_merge_commit_title = PR_TITLE`, so the squash always uses the PR title. This also means the commit body is blank, so only the title can carry the breaking marker. The spec now says this.
- **Close PR #363.** It is already closed.
- **The `release-plz.toml` comment about `dependencies_update`.** It is out of scope and does not change this design.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

# jiff 1 upgrade Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Move the workspace to jiff `1` and make release-plz release it as a minor bump of `paigasus-helikon-core` and the facade `paigasus-helikon`.

**Architecture:** A dependency-requirement change in the root `Cargo.toml`, a lockfile update, upgrade notes in two CHANGELOGs, and one new compatibility test in core. The minor bump comes from the `!` in the squash title, which release-plz gives to the two crates whose directories the commit touches. A scratch-clone `release-plz update` run proves the bump before the PR.

**Tech Stack:** Rust 1.94+ workspace, jiff, serde_json, release-plz CLI v0.4.3, cargo-semver-checks.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-20-jiff-1-upgrade-design.md`

All paths are relative to the worktree root
`/Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-831`.
Guard every `cd` with `|| exit 1`. Never run `git checkout <branch>`,
`git switch`, `git reset --hard`, or `git stash` in this worktree. Work in the
foreground until each command has a final status.

## Global Constraints

- jiff requirement: `jiff = { version = "1", features = ["serde"] }` in root `Cargo.toml` `[workspace.dependencies]`. No exact pin (SMA-818).
- `Cargo.lock` has jiff 1.x only (jiff, jiff-core, jiff-static, jiff-tzdb, jiff-tzdb-platform).
- No source change outside the new test file. The probe proved the workspace compiles as is.
- Allowed diff: root `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `crates/paigasus-helikon-core/CHANGELOG.md`, `crates/paigasus-helikon/CHANGELOG.md`, `crates/paigasus-helikon-core/tests/jiff_wire_compat.rs`, `docs/superpowers/`. No other `crates/*` path.
- Each branch commit that touches a CHANGELOG uses a `!` type.
- PR title: `chore(deps)!: SMA-831 upgrade jiff to 1`.
- Target versions: core 0.6.0 → 0.7.0, facade 0.6.14 → 0.7.0. Every other changed crate gets a patch.
- All user-facing text (CHANGELOG notes, comments) is in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English.
- Do not touch the five `trybuild_ui` mismatches. They fail on clean `main` with local rustc 1.99.0.

## Review Focus

1. A stored `ts` with nine fractional digits must read back and write back to the same bytes. Covered: Task 1 `nanosecond_ts_keeps_its_bytes`.
2. jiff writes the shortest fractional part (`.5`, not `.500000000`). A row written that way must keep its bytes. Covered: Task 1 `trimmed_fraction_ts_keeps_its_bytes`.
3. A whole-second `ts` has no fractional part. Covered: Task 1 `whole_second_ts_keeps_its_bytes`.
4. A row that another writer stored with a `+00:00` offset must still parse to the same instant. Covered: Task 1 `utc_offset_ts_parses`.
5. The `build-no-default-features` gate compiles crates with default features off. jiff 1 must not need a default feature that the workspace turns off. Covered: Task 2 Step 6.

---

### Task 1: Pin the stored timestamp format on jiff 0.2

**Files:**
- Revert: `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` (the uncommitted probe edit)
- Create: `crates/paigasus-helikon-core/tests/jiff_wire_compat.rs`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `paigasus_helikon_core::{SessionEvent, ContentPart}`, `jiff::Timestamp`.
- Produces: the test binary `jiff_wire_compat`, which Task 2 runs again on jiff 1.

- [ ] **Step 1: Remove the probe edit**

Run: `git restore Cargo.toml Cargo.lock && grep -n '^jiff' Cargo.toml`
Expected: `jiff                  = { version = "0.2.46", features = ["serde"] }`, and `git status --porcelain` lists only `docs/superpowers/` files.

- [ ] **Step 2: Write the test file**

Module doc: the file pins the JSON form of `SessionEvent.ts`, as jiff 0.2 writes it, so that a jiff major upgrade cannot change stored session rows (SMA-831).

One helper: `fn assert_bytes_kept(json: &str, expected_ts: Timestamp)`. It deserializes `json` (compact, one line) into `SessionEvent`, asserts that the event's `ts()` equals `expected_ts`, serializes it again with `serde_json::to_string`, and asserts that the result equals `json` byte for byte.

Each test uses a `user_message` event with one text part `"hi"`. The JSON shape is `{"type":"user_message","content":[{"type":"text","text":"hi"}],"ts":"<TS>"}`.

| Test | `<TS>` | `expected_ts` |
|---|---|---|
| `nanosecond_ts_keeps_its_bytes` | `2026-11-20T15:08:42.123456789Z` | `Timestamp::new(1_795_187_322, 123_456_789)` |
| `trimmed_fraction_ts_keeps_its_bytes` | `2026-11-20T15:08:42.5Z` | `Timestamp::new(1_795_187_322, 500_000_000)` |
| `whole_second_ts_keeps_its_bytes` | `2026-11-20T15:08:42Z` | `Timestamp::new(1_795_187_322, 0)` |

`utc_offset_ts_parses` is different. It deserializes the same JSON with `<TS>` = `2026-11-20T15:08:42.123456789+00:00` and asserts only that `ts()` equals `Timestamp::new(1_795_187_322, 123_456_789)`. A writer can store a `+00:00` offset, and jiff re-serializes it as `Z`, so a byte check is not correct here.

If the JSON field order from `serde_json::to_string` differs from the shape above, take the order from the existing snapshot `tests/snapshots/serde_roundtrip__session_event_user_message_roundtrip.snap` and use it in all four strings.

- [ ] **Step 3: Run the tests on jiff 0.2**

This is a characterization test, so it passes the first time. It must pass on jiff 0.2, because that proves that the literals are real 0.2 output.
Run: `cargo test -p paigasus-helikon-core --test jiff_wire_compat`
Expected: `test result: ok. 4 passed`. If a byte test fails, the literal is not what jiff 0.2 writes. Correct the literal to the 0.2 output, and record the change in the task report. Do not change the assertion.

- [ ] **Step 4: Format, lint, commit**

Run: `cargo fmt --all && cargo clippy -p paigasus-helikon-core --all-features --tests -- -D warnings`
Expected: no diff from fmt after the run, and clippy exits 0.

```bash
git add crates/paigasus-helikon-core/tests/jiff_wire_compat.rs
git commit -m "test(core): SMA-831 pin the stored timestamp format before the jiff 1 upgrade"
```

---

### Task 2: Upgrade jiff to 1, with the upgrade notes

**Files:**
- Modify: `Cargo.toml:49-53` (the jiff comment and requirement)
- Modify: `Cargo.lock`
- Modify: `crates/paigasus-helikon-core/CHANGELOG.md` (under `## [Unreleased]`)
- Modify: `crates/paigasus-helikon/CHANGELOG.md` (under `## [Unreleased]`)

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: the `jiff_wire_compat` test from Task 1.
- Produces: the branch state that Task 3 squashes and checks.

- [ ] **Step 1: Change the requirement and the comment**

Set the line to `jiff                  = { version = "1", features = ["serde"] }` (keep the column alignment). Replace lines 49-52 with a comment that says: a caret requirement, not an exact pin, because an exact pin goes into every published manifest and blocks consumers that need a newer jiff (SMA-818); `jiff::Timestamp` is public API of core (`SessionEvent.ts`), so the next jiff major is a breaking change of core and the facade, and its PR title must carry `!` (SMA-831). Do not keep the 0.2.29 / RUSTSEC-2026-0173 text.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/smaschek/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/7.0.2/skills/subagent-driven-development

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "executing-plans" [label="yes"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="no"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (inline):**
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution) instead of one context doing every task
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality) instead of only at the end
- Costs a fresh context per task and per review; inline costs one context plus one final reviewer
- Both run in this session, share the same plan workspace and ledger, and never pause between tasks

## The Process

```dot
digraph process {
    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];
        "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];
        "Generate review package, dispatch task reviewer (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" [shape=diamond];
        "Fix loop: read references/fix-loop.md before every round" [shape=box];
        "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" [shape=box];
    }

    "Setup: worktree, ledger check, read plan, pre-flight review" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Final review and finish: read references/final-review.md" [shape=box];
    "Final review clean: delete this plan's workspace" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Setup: worktree, ledger check, read plan, pre-flight review" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" -> "Implementer asks questions?";
    "Implementer asks questions?" -> "Answer questions, provide context" [label="yes"];
    "Answer questions, provide context" -> "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews";
    "Implementer asks questions?" -> "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [label="no"];
    "Implementer implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" -> "Generate review package, dispatch task reviewer (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)";
    "Generate review package, dispatch task reviewer (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Spec ✅ and quality approved?";
    "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" [label="yes"];
    "Spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Fix loop: read references/fix-loop.md before every round" [label="no"];
    "Fix loop: read references/fix-loop.md before every round" -> "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" [label="addressed, or parked at the cap"];
    "Append completion to ledger, mark todo complete" -> "More tasks remain?";
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Final review and finish: read references/final-review.md" [label="no"];
    "Final review and finish: read references/final-review.md" -> "Final review clean: delete this plan's workspace";
    "Final review clean: delete this plan's workspace" -> "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch";
}
```

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` by its absolute path, from the
  working tree you're executing in — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (under `<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If one exists,
  read [references/resuming.md](references/resuming.md) before anything
  else: it says whose ledger it is and where to resume.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

Before dispatching Task 1, read [references/preflight.md](references/preflight.md)
and run the conflict scan it describes. Its table and rulings go in the
ledger.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

**Small same-shape work:** when the plan lists several small edits of the
same kind across files, read [references/batching.md](references/batching.md)
before dispatching them.

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

**Waiting on dispatched subagents:** never poll a wait interface with
short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either.
While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review,
reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own.
When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten
minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one
line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase
any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly
all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost
child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `bash scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` by its absolute path, from the
  working tree you're executing in — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
  review seat per task.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` by its absolute path, from the working tree you're executing in — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**Any other status** (DONE_WITH_CONCERNS, NEEDS_CONTEXT, BLOCKED): read
[references/handling-reports.md](references/handling-reports.md) and follow
it, every time you get one.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` by its absolute path, from
  the working tree you're executing in, and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## When to Use

```dot

    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [shape=diamond];

    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "executing-plans" [label="yes"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="no"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (inline):**
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution) instead of one context doing every task
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality) instead of only at the end
- Costs a fresh context per task and per review; inline costs one context plus one final reviewer
- Both run in this session, share the same plan workspace and ledger, and never pause between tasks

partner's explicit consent.

controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

  working tree you're executing in — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (under `<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.

  read [references/resuming.md](references/resuming.md) before anything
  else: it says whose ledger it is and where to resume.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.

  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.

rulings made without one are provisional.

ledger.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.

implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —

- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

# Implementer Subagent Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching an implementer subagent.

```
Subagent (general-purpose):
  description: "Implement Task N: [task name]"
  model: [MODEL — REQUIRED: choose per SKILL.md Model Selection; an omitted
         model silently inherits the session's most expensive one]
  prompt: |
    You are implementing Task N: [task name]

    ## Task Description

    Read your task brief first: [BRIEF_FILE]
    It contains the full task text from the plan.

    ## Context

    [Scene-setting: where this fits, dependencies, architectural context]

    ## Before You Begin

    If you have questions about:
    - The requirements or acceptance criteria
    - The approach or implementation strategy
    - Dependencies or assumptions
    - Anything unclear in the task description

    **Ask them now.** Raise any concerns before starting work.

    ## Your Job

    Once you're clear on requirements:
    1. Implement exactly what the task specifies
    2. Write tests (following TDD if task says to)
    3. Verify implementation works
    4. Commit your work
    5. Self-review (see below)
    6. Report back

    Work from: [directory]

    **While you work:** If you encounter something unexpected or unclear, **ask questions**.
    It's always OK to pause and clarify. Don't guess or make assumptions.

    While iterating, run the focused test for what you're changing; run the
    full suite once before committing, not after every edit.

    ## You Do Not Dispatch Subagents

    Do all of this task's work yourself. Never spawn a subagent to
    implement part of the task, and above all never spawn a reviewer to
    check your work. Self-review (below) means reading your own diff.
    Review is the controller's job: after you report, it dispatches a
    fresh reviewer against your diff. A reviewer you spawn duplicates
    that review at full cost, and its approval counts for nothing in
    the process. If you catch yourself thinking "an independent review
    would strengthen my report" — that review is already scheduled.
    Report instead.

    ## Code Organization

    You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more
    reliable when files are focused. Keep this in mind:
    - Follow the file structure defined in the plan
    - Each file should have one clear responsibility with a well-defined interface
    - If a file you're creating is growing beyond the plan's intent, stop and report
      it as DONE_WITH_CONCERNS — don't split files on your own without plan guidance
    - If an existing file you're modifying is already large or tangled, work carefully
      and note it as a concern in your report
    - In existing codebases, follow established patterns. Improve code you're touching
      the way a good developer would, but don't restructure things outside your task.

    ## When You're in Over Your Head

    It is always OK to stop and say "this is too hard for me." Bad work is worse than
    no work. You will not be penalized for escalating.

    **STOP and escalate when:**
    - The task requires architectural decisions with multiple valid approaches
    - You need to understand code beyond what was provided and can't find clarity
    - You feel uncertain about whether your approach is correct
    - The task involves restructuring existing code in ways the plan didn't anticipate
    - You've been reading file after file trying to understand the system without progress

    **How to escalate:** Report back with status BLOCKED or NEEDS_CONTEXT. Describe
    specifically what you're stuck on, what you've tried, and what kind of help you need.
    The controller can provide more context, re-dispatch with a more capable model,
    or break the task into smaller pieces.

    ## Before Reporting Back: Self-Review

    Review your work with fresh eyes. Ask yourself:

    **Completeness:**
    - Did I fully implement everything in the spec?
    - Did I miss any requirements?
    - Are there edge cases I didn't handle?

    **Quality:**
    - Is this my best work?
    - Are names clear and accurate (match what things do, not how they work)?
    - Is the code clean and maintainable?

    **Discipline:**
    - Did I avoid overbuilding (YAGNI)?
    - Did I only build what was requested?
    - Did I follow existing patterns in the codebase?

    **Testing:**
    - Do tests actually verify behavior (not just mock behavior)?
    - Did I follow TDD if required?
    - Are tests comprehensive?
    - Is the test output pristine (no stray warnings or noise)?

    If you find issues during self-review, fix them now before reporting.

    ## After Review Findings

    If the task review finds issues, you will be resumed with the findings.
    Fix them, re-run the tests that cover the amended code, and append a fix
    report to your report file: what you changed, the covering tests you
    ran, the command, and the output. Reviewers will not re-run tests for
    you — your report is the test evidence. Then reply with the same short
    status contract as your first report.

    ## Report Format

    Write your full report to [REPORT_FILE]:
    - What you implemented (or what you attempted, if blocked)
    - What you tested and test results
    - **TDD Evidence** (if TDD was required for this task):
      - RED: command run, relevant failing output before implementation, and why the failure was expected
      - GREEN: command run and relevant passing output after implementation
    - Files changed
    - Self-review findings (if any)
    - Any issues or concerns

    Then report back with ONLY (under 15 lines — the detail lives in the
    report file):
    - **Status:** DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED | NEEDS_CONTEXT
    - Commits created (short SHA + subject)
    - One-line test summary (e.g. "14/14 passing, output pristine")
    - Your concerns, if any
    - The report file path

    If BLOCKED or NEEDS_CONTEXT, put the specifics in the final message
    itself — the controller acts on it directly.

    Use DONE_WITH_CONCERNS if you completed the work but have doubts about correctness.
    Use BLOCKED if you cannot complete the task. Use NEEDS_CONTEXT if you need
    information that wasn't provided. Never silently produce work you're unsure about.
```

# Task Reviewer Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching a task reviewer subagent. The reviewer
reads the task's diff once and returns two verdicts: spec compliance and
code quality.

**Purpose:** Verify one task's implementation matches its requirements (nothing
more, nothing less) and is well-built (clean, tested, maintainable)

```
Subagent (general-purpose):
  description: "Review Task N (spec + quality)"
  model: [MODEL — REQUIRED: choose per SKILL.md Model Selection; an omitted
         model silently inherits the session's most expensive one]
  prompt: |
    You are reviewing one task's implementation: first whether it matches its
    requirements, then whether it is well-built. This is a task-scoped gate,
    not a merge review — a broad whole-branch review happens separately after
    all tasks are complete.

    ## What Was Requested

    Read the task brief: [BRIEF_FILE]

    Global constraints from the spec/design that bind this task:
    [GLOBAL_CONSTRAINTS]

    ## What the Implementer Claims They Built

    Read the implementer's report: [REPORT_FILE]

    ## Diff Under Review

    **Base:** [BASE_SHA]
    **Head:** [HEAD_SHA]
    **Diff file:** [DIFF_FILE]

    Read the diff file once — it contains the commit list, a stat summary,
    and the full diff with surrounding context, and it is your view of the
    change. The diff's context lines ARE the changed files: do not Read a
    changed file separately unless a hunk you must judge is cut off
    mid-function — and say so in your report. Do not re-run git commands.
    If the diff file is missing, fetch the diff yourself:
    `git diff --stat [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]` and `git diff [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]`.
    Do not crawl the broader codebase. Inspect code outside the diff only
    to evaluate a concrete risk you can name — one focused check per named
    risk, and name both the risk and what you checked in your report.
    Cross-cutting changes are legitimate named risks: if the diff changes
    lock ordering, a function or API contract, or shared mutable state,
    checking the call sites is the right method.

    Your review is read-only on this checkout. Do not mutate the working
    tree, the index, HEAD, or branch state in any way.

    ## You Do Not Dispatch Subagents

    Do all of this review yourself. Never spawn a subagent to review part
    of the diff, and never spawn another reviewer for a second opinion.
    This process already provides every review seat the work gets; a
    reviewer you spawn duplicates one of them at full cost, and its
    verdict counts for nothing. If the diff feels too large for one
    pass, review it in passes yourself and say so in your report.

    ## Do Not Trust the Report

    Treat the implementer's report as unverified claims about the code. It
    may be incomplete, inaccurate, or optimistic. Verify the claims against
    the diff. Design rationales in the report are claims too: "left it per
    YAGNI," "kept it simple deliberately," or any other justification is the
    implementer grading their own work. Judge the code on its merits — a
    stated rationale never downgrades a finding's severity.

    ## Tests

    The implementer already ran the tests and reported results with TDD
    evidence for exactly this code. Do not re-run the suite to confirm their
    report. Run a test only when reading the code raises a specific doubt
    that no existing run answers — and then a focused test, never a
    package-wide suite, race detector run, or repeated/high-count loop. If
    heavy validation seems warranted, recommend it in your report instead of
```

### Upgrade notes

- This release requires `jiff` 1. The `ts` fields of `SessionEvent` and the return value of `SessionEvent::ts()` now have the type `jiff::Timestamp` from jiff 1. A `Timestamp` from jiff 0.2 is a different type.

- If your code uses only the constructors that set `ts` to the current time (for example `SessionEvent::user_message`) and does not read `ts`, it needs no change.
- Upgrade `paigasus-helikon-core` and `paigasus-helikon` to 0.7 together. If your lockfile keeps `paigasus-helikon` 0.6 after `cargo update`, it can hold two copies of core. Run `cargo tree -d -i paigasus-helikon-core` to find them.

# Final Review and Finish

Part of superpowers:subagent-driven-development. Every task in the plan is
complete.

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` by its absolute path,
from the working tree you're executing in (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see SKILL.md's Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`bash scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` by its absolute path,
from the working tree you're executing in, over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](../re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the fix loop's breaker
(references/fix-loop.md): park with rulings, or rule on the load-bearing
ones and ledger what you decided. Only the four things that stop a running
plan (top of SKILL.md) stop you here. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

### Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing `Ruling:` —
preflight rulings, parked findings, breaker adjudications, all of them — into
your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you made them, each
with what it costs if wrong. The list is exhaustive: if the ledger holds a
ruling, the list holds it. That list is the only place the decisions you
took on your human partner's behalf reach them — they read it and rework
whatever you got wrong. A ruling that dies with the workspace was a decision
made in secret.

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.
